stem: Which measure of center and spread is most appropriate to report for this distribution, and why?
stimulus: A researcher records the time (in minutes) that 40 customers spend in a coffee shop. The distribution of times is strongly right-skewed, with a few customers staying much longer than typical. The five-number summary is: Min = 3, Q1 = 8, Median = 12, Q3 = 18, Max = 65.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.
choices.rationale: Both the mean and standard deviation are pulled toward the long right tail and the high outlier (65); they are not resistant, so 'uses every value' is not a reason to prefer them for a skewed distribution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.
choices.rationale: The range is determined entirely by the two most extreme values, making it even more sensitive to the outlier than the standard deviation; the mean is also not resistant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.
choices.rationale: The median and IQR depend only on the middle portion of the ordered data, so they are not distorted by the skew or the outlier at 65 minutes -- the standard choice for a skewed distribution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.
choices.rationale: This mixes a resistant measure of center with a non-resistant measure of spread; shape and outliers affect standard deviation just as much as they affect the mean.

stem: What is the standard deviation of T?
stimulus: A vending machine dispenses two independent snack items in a bundle. The number of chip bags dispensed has mean 3 and standard deviation 0.8. The number of candy bars dispensed has mean 2 and standard deviation 0.6. Let T = total number of snack items (chips + candy) dispensed in a bundle.

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1.4, because standard deviations of independent random variables add directly.
choices.rationale: Standard deviations do not add directly, even for independent random variables; it is the variances that add.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.2, because the standard deviation of a sum is the difference of the standard deviations.
choices.rationale: This applies the wrong operation entirely; subtracting standard deviations has no statistical justification here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1.96, because the variance of T is the square of the sum of the two standard deviations.
choices.rationale: This squares the sum of the standard deviations (0.8 + 0.6)^2 instead of summing the individual variances, a common algebra-of-variance error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.0, because Var(T) = 0.8^2 + 0.6^2 = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) is the square root of 1.00.
choices.rationale: For independent random variables, variances add: Var(T) = Var(chips) + Var(candy) = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) = sqrt(1.00) = 1.0.

stem: Which pair of summary statistics is most appropriate to describe the center and spread?
stimulus: A set of delivery times is strongly right-skewed, with a few very long times.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use all the data values.
choices.rationale: Using every value is not an advantage when the distribution is skewed; these measures are not resistant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the overall spread.
choices.rationale: The range is driven only by the extreme values and is extremely sensitive to outliers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the skew and the long right tail.
choices.rationale: Median and IQR are resistant measures, so they are the standard choice for skewed distributions and outliers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant.
choices.rationale: This mixes a resistant center with a non-resistant spread measure.

stem: Which measure is most resistant to the outlier 40?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Range
choices.rationale: The range is entirely determined by the minimum and maximum, so it is not resistant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard deviation
choices.rationale: Standard deviation is pulled by extreme values and is not resistant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: IQR
choices.rationale: IQR depends on the middle half of the ordered data and is resistant to a single extreme value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean
choices.rationale: The mean is also not resistant to outliers.

stimulus: A distribution is roughly symmetric with no outliers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean must be much larger than the median.
choices.rationale: That would suggest right skew, not symmetry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The median must always be larger than the mean.
choices.rationale: There is no such rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean and median will be close to each other.
choices.rationale: In a roughly symmetric distribution, mean and median tend to be similar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The range is always the best measure of spread.
choices.rationale: The best measure depends on shape and outliers.

stimulus: An experiment compares two diets, but age may affect results.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ignore age because random assignment always eliminates all variation.
choices.rationale: Random assignment reduces confounding but does not remove all variation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Group subjects into age categories before random assignment within each age block.
choices.rationale: Blocking controls a known source of variability by balancing it across treatments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use convenience sampling instead.
choices.rationale: Convenience sampling increases bias and does not block anything.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the largest age group only.
choices.rationale: This would discard data and does not properly block.

stimulus: A medical trial is designed so neither the subjects nor the evaluators know who receives the pill or placebo.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It guarantees the treatment works.
choices.rationale: Blinding does not guarantee effectiveness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It helps reduce placebo effects and observer bias.
choices.rationale: Blinding reduces the chance that expectations affect responses or measurements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment.
choices.rationale: Random assignment is still needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes the sample larger.
choices.rationale: Blinding does not change sample size.

stem: What is the probability of success on both stages?
stimulus: A two-stage process has P(first success) = 0.3 and P(second success | first success) = 0.5.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This adds probabilities instead of multiplying along the path.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Multiply along the path: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Multiplies 0.7 (the probability the first stage does not succeed) by 0.5 instead of 0.3 by 0.5: 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.35.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Treats the two probabilities as overlapping events and adds them, 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65, instead of multiplying 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15 for both stages succeeding.

stem: What features are needed for a binomial setting?
stimulus: A basketball player makes a free throw with probability 0.7 on each attempt.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any random experiment with numerical outcomes.
choices.rationale: Not every random experiment is binomial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fixed number of trials, independent trials, two outcomes per trial, and a constant success probability.
choices.rationale: Those are the standard binomial conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least three outcomes on each trial.
choices.rationale: Binomial trials have only two outcomes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A changing success probability from trial to trial.
choices.rationale: Constant p is required.

topic: 4.2 (registered; content is a proportion CI, so 3.3)
stem: What happens if the sample size increases and all else stays the same?
stimulus: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion has margin of error 0.04.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The margin of error gets larger.
choices.rationale: That is the opposite of the sample-size effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The margin of error stays exactly the same.
choices.rationale: Sample size affects SE and MOE.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The margin of error gets smaller.
choices.rationale: Larger samples reduce standard error, which shrinks the margin of error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The margin of error becomes negative.
choices.rationale: Margins of error are never negative.

stem: What is the power of the test?
stimulus: A study has β = 0.25 for a particular test.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: That is β, the Type II error rate.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Power = 1 - β = 0.75.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: That would be α in many settings, not power.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is not 1 - β here.

stem: Which formula correctly finds P(machine B | defective)?
stimulus: A factory has three machines with different defect rates and production shares.

choices.label: A
choices.text: P(B)P(defective)
choices.rationale: This is not conditional probability; it omits the denominator.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P(B | defective) = P(B) / P(defective | B)
choices.rationale: That is not Bayes’ theorem.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P(defective | B) + P(B)
choices.rationale: Probabilities are not combined this way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P(defective | B)P(B) / P(defective)
choices.rationale: Bayes’ theorem reverses the conditional probability using the defect probability in the numerator and the total defect probability in the denominator.

stimulus: A random variable takes values 1, 2, and 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This likely comes from a rough average rather than the weighted mean.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the correct weighted average.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the largest outcome, not the mean.
